ar_whitcombs_the.blurb: A quiet boulder field in the forested hills of the Arkansas River Valley, reached from the town of Hollis. The stone is harder and less grippy than the sandstone farther north in the state, so friction and good technique matter. All of the climbing is bouldering, with a broad spread of difficulty: a handful of easy problems, a big middle band from about V2 to V5, and a few V6 to V8 lines. Tofurkey, Shots Fired and Gun Control are the standouts. Development is still young and the place sees few visitors, so expect to route-find between boulders, and give the rock a day or two to dry after rain.
ar_whitcombs_the.parking_note: From Hollis, go north on Highway 7 for a mile or two, turn right on Whitcomb Road, then take the first right onto the rougher forest road. A low-water bridge comes early. Drive on to a large clearing in the trees if your vehicle has the clearance; otherwise park part-way and walk.
ar_whitcombs_the.approach: From the clearing, climb the slope along its right-hand side until the ground flattens, then angle up and right into the woods. The boulders are a few minutes further.

bc_hassler_crag.blurb: A secluded sandstone and conglomerate cliff in northern British Columbia, west of Chetwynd beside Highway 97. Walls run roughly 20 m high and carry a mix of trad, sport, top-rope and bouldering. Trad is the largest share, and the roped grades cluster around 5.10 and 5.11, with a thinner spread of easier climbs from 5.6 to 5.9. The boulder problems are mostly V0 to V5. Self Service Pump is the sport standout. Much of the rock catches sun through the afternoon, and the crag is remote, so bring everything you need and plan for a long drive from any sizeable town.
bc_hassler_crag.parking_note: Park beside Highway 97 about 20 km west of Chetwynd, across the highway from Houde Road.

bc_perry_creek.blurb: A compact talus slide of quartzite boulders in the East Kootenays, across the road from the Perry Creek sport crag. The problems are steep and athletic, with slopers, big incuts and gymnastic movement, and the landings are mostly good talus that climbers have built up. Most of the climbing sits between V0 and V3, with a decent number of V4 to V6 problems and a couple of harder lines. The trail from the parking area reaches the first boulders in under a minute, and more problems sit higher in the slide. The surrounding forest is dry, so keep fires well away from the rocks.
bc_perry_creek.parking_note: From Highway 95A between Kimberley and Cranbrook, follow Wycliffe Park Road, Old Wycliffe Road, Perry Creek Road and then the Booth Creek forest road, keeping left at forks. The last stretch is rough but passable in a regular car. Park at the main lot beside the slide.
bc_perry_creek.approach: A clear trail enters the talus in about 30 seconds. Cairns lead up to the cave problems, and a couple of boulders sit two minutes across the grassy slope.

bc_lakit_lake.blurb: A steep sport crag of pale quartzite beside a small lake near Cranbrook, in the East Kootenays. Climbs are one pitch and demanding, with slopey ledges, crimps and big bubble-shaped jugs that build a serious forearm pump. Few routes are easy: the bulk of the climbing is 5.11 and 5.12, with a smaller group of 5.10s and a few at 5.13 and above, so it suits climbers already comfortable on harder sport. G.I. Joe, Kamikaze and Mayday are among the best known. A campsite sits next to the parking area, which makes it a popular overnight stop.
bc_lakit_lake.parking_note: From Cranbrook, drive north past Fort Steele to Lakit Lake Road and turn right, then follow signs along dirt roads for several kilometres to the campsite and parking lot at the end.

bc_the_arena.blurb: The largest group of boulders in The Grid, a bouldering zone in the Hunter Creek area near Hope. Problems cover nearly the whole range, from V0 up to a V10, with most falling between V2 and V6 and a good number of V7 to V9 lines for stronger climbers. Drug Fueled Romance, Gem and Younger and Frailer are among the favorites. The approach follows a gated road and a faint trail through the trees, so expect some searching on a first visit. Hope's boulders see far fewer people than Squamish, but the land around them is private, so be quiet, tidy and take all your garbage out.
bc_the_arena.parking_note: Take exit 160 off Highway 1 and head up Hunter Creek Road to its end. Leave the car below the short rise near the locked gate, clear of both the gate and the road.
bc_the_arena.approach: Go around the gate and stay on the main gravel track as it swings right, doubling back almost 180 degrees, to an open power-line cut with a rough driveway into the trees. A faint trail runs east from the driveway into the boulders.

bc_the_kelowna_boulderfields.blurb: A large field of gneiss boulders on the hillside south of Kelowna, among the better-known bouldering areas in the interior of British Columbia. The rock is steep and varied, with power lines, caves, technical faces, sloping traverses and some highballs. The problems in this part lean easy to moderate, mostly V0 to V4 with a few harder ones, and the wider area holds many more at every level. Getting there means a dirt road and then a hike of up to about twenty minutes. Spring and autumn are the usual seasons, and the open slope can be hot in summer.

bc_burgers_and_fries.blurb: One of the busiest and most approachable cliffs in the Smoke Bluffs, the small granite crags on the edge of Squamish. Most of the climbing is short trad, with some sport and top-rope. Grades run from 5.5 through 5.12, concentrated around 5.6 to 5.7 and again at 5.10 to 5.11, which makes it a favorite for new leaders and for climbing courses. The left side gets much more sun and wind and dries quickly, while the right side is shadier under tree cover. Expect crowds on dry weekends, and watch for seepage in spots after wet weather.
bc_burgers_and_fries.parking_note: Use the climbers' lot for the Smoke Bluffs and walk in from there rather than parking on the residential streets.

bc_aspen_pillars.blurb: A section of the Aberdeen Columns, a cliff of dark basalt columns on the plateau above Vernon in the Okanagan. All of the climbing here is trad, on steep, straight-sided cracks that range from fingers to wide, up to about 25 m high. Grades run from easy to 5.10, with the largest groups at 5.7 to 5.9. Protection is generally good with cams, though lightly used routes can have loose rock and lichen. There are no bolts, and tree or chain anchors are used at the top. Mosquitoes and black flies can be bothersome in early summer, and stinging nettles grow along the trail.
bc_aspen_pillars.parking_note: From Vernon, head east on Highway 6 to Lavington, then follow the signed roads up to the Aberdeen forest road, then the Aberdeen-Haddo Lake and Goat Creek forest roads. Park just past the corner at about 18 km.
bc_aspen_pillars.approach: A signed trail leaves the east side of the road and runs through the trees to the cliff.
